prompt: Which part of Fabric is created as a resource in an Azure subscription?
hint: It is the part that has a size and a price per hour.

choices.text: The capacity, in a subscription and a region
choices.why: Right. It is created in a subscription and a region, with a size from F2 to F2048; everything else lives inside Fabric.

choices.text: Each workspace, with its members
choices.why: A workspace is created inside Fabric and assigned to a capacity; Azure Resource Manager does not know it.

choices.text: Every lakehouse and every warehouse
choices.why: They are items inside a workspace, managed in the Fabric portal.

choices.text: OneLake, once per region
choices.why: OneLake comes with the tenant, one for all of it, and nobody provisions it.

prompt: Quitanda puts its development workspace and its production workspace on two separate capacities. What does that separate?
hint: There is still one OneLake.

choices.text: The data: each capacity has a OneLake of its own, so development cannot read production
choices.why: There is one OneLake per tenant, whatever the capacities; a shortcut can read across them.

choices.text: The bill, and the noise one makes in the other
choices.why: Right. A heavy notebook in development spends its own capacity and cannot throttle production's reports.

choices.text: The sign-in: each capacity belongs to its own Entra ID tenant
choices.why: Both capacities are in the same tenant; a tenant has one Fabric.

choices.text: Nothing at all; a capacity is only a label on the bill
choices.why: A capacity is the compute itself, and its size limits what runs on it.

prompt: A platform team wants its whole Fabric setup declared with the `azurerm` provider for Terraform. What of it can `azurerm` declare?
hint: Only one part of Fabric is an Azure resource.

choices.text: The capacity, the workspaces and the lakehouses
choices.why: Workspaces and lakehouses are managed inside Fabric, not by Azure Resource Manager.

choices.text: Nothing, since Fabric is not sold through Azure
choices.why: The capacity is an Azure resource, and the lesson validates one.

choices.text: The capacity, and nothing that lives in its workspaces
choices.why: Right. `azurerm_fabric_capacity` is the one resource; what lives in the workspaces is outside `azurerm`.

choices.text: Everything, if each item gets a resource group
choices.why: Items have no resource group; they belong to a workspace.

prompt: At the lesson's illustrative 0.20 USD per CU-hour, what does an F8 cost for a 730-hour month running all the time, in USD?
hint: CUs, times the price, times the hours.

prompt: Quitanda's F32 capacity reaches interactive rejection every week, and it is decided to size up. What is the next size?
hint: Look at the list the provider printed.

choices.why: There is no F40: each size doubles the one before.
There is no F48 either; the list goes F32, F64.
Right. Growing is a step to twice the size, and twice the price.
Sizes are not counted one CU at a time.

prompt: A capacity has carried forward 90 minutes of future consumption. Somebody opens a report, and the nightly notebook starts. What happens to each?
hint: Between 60 minutes and 24 hours.

choices.text: Both run, and the report's queries wait 20 seconds before they start
choices.why: That is the interactive delay stage, from 10 to 60 minutes; 90 is past it.

choices.text: The report is refused and the notebook runs
choices.why: Right. From 60 minutes to 24 hours new interactive requests are rejected, and background work still runs.

choices.text: The report and the notebook are both refused until the debt is paid
choices.why: Background work is refused only past 24 hours of future consumption.

choices.text: Neither the report nor the notebook notices; throttling starts at 24 hours
choices.why: Throttling starts after 10 minutes; 24 hours is where background work is refused too.

prompt: An administrator pauses a throttled pay-as-you-go capacity to make the throttling stop. What does Microsoft's documentation say happens to the consumption it had carried forward?
hint: Pausing stops the meter from now on.

choices.text: It is forgiven, which is why pausing is the documented remedy
choices.why: Nothing is forgiven; work already done was consumption.

choices.text: It is added to the bill at the moment the capacity is paused
choices.why: Right. A capacity paused to escape throttling pays for what it had already spent.

choices.text: It waits, and is paid back from idle time after the capacity resumes
choices.why: The documentation says it is billed when the capacity is paused, not kept for later.

choices.text: It moves to another capacity in the same tenant
choices.why: Consumption belongs to the capacity that did the work.

prompt: Fabric spreads the consumption of a background operation, such as a scheduled notebook, over ___ hours.
hint: A whole day.

prompt: OneLake answers the ADLS Gen2 interface. Which of these can read Quitanda's lakehouse with nothing changed but the address and the sign-in? Choose all that apply.
hint: Anything that already speaks ADLS Gen2 with an Entra ID identity.

choices.text: Spark, reading an `abfss://` path
choices.why: Yes: the path names onelake.dfs.fabric.microsoft.com.

choices.text: `azcopy`
choices.why: Yes, with an Entra ID sign-in.

choices.text: The Azure SDK for Python
choices.why: Yes, through its Data Lake or blob client.

choices.text: `az storage blob list` with the account key
choices.why: OneLake has no account, so it has no account key; access is by identity.

prompt: Quitanda's lakehouse has a shortcut to a partner's Amazon S3 bucket, and a notebook reads it every hour. What does the shortcut avoid, and what does it not?
hint: Nothing is copied, so where does each read go?

choices.text: It avoids S3's requests and egress, since Fabric reads over Microsoft's own network
choices.why: The bytes leave Amazon's cloud whatever network carries them, and Amazon charges for that.

choices.text: It avoids a copy; each read is still a read from S3, with its requests and egress
choices.why: Right. A shortcut points rather than copies, so the bill at the other end is still there.

choices.text: It avoids nothing, since it is a copy into OneLake made on a schedule
choices.why: That describes a pipeline, not a shortcut.

choices.text: It avoids the credential, because Fabric reads S3 with the reader's own identity
choices.why: A shortcut to S3 reaches it with a credential kept in a Fabric connection.

prompt: A shortcut to Quitanda's exports uses a connection whose service principal may read the whole storage account, contracts included. Analysts may use the shortcut. What is wrong?
hint: Whose rights does a read through the shortcut use?

choices.text: The credential reaches the contracts too, and so does any shortcut made with it
choices.why: Right. A read through a shortcut uses the connection's rights, so that principal should read the exports folder and nothing more.

choices.text: The analysts read through it with their own rights, so they get an error
choices.why: A shortcut reaches the source with the connection's credential, not each reader's.

choices.text: The shortcut copies the whole account, contracts included, into OneLake
choices.why: A shortcut copies nothing.

choices.text: Shortcuts accept only account keys, so the principal is ignored
choices.why: A connection can use a service principal, among other credentials.

prompt: An analyst runs `INSERT INTO orders` through a lakehouse's SQL analytics endpoint. What happens?
hint: Who owns a lakehouse's tables?

choices.text: The endpoint adds the row, as any T-SQL database would
choices.why: The endpoint lets T-SQL read a lakehouse's tables, not write them.

choices.text: It is refused, because that endpoint only reads
choices.why: Right. The tables belong to Spark; a warehouse is where T-SQL writes.

choices.text: It is turned into a Spark job, which adds the row a few minutes later
choices.why: Nothing translates T-SQL writes into Spark.

choices.text: The row goes to the `Files` area, as a CSV
choices.why: `Files` is written by whoever puts files there, not by SQL.

prompt: Each night Quitanda loads the orders, their items and the day's summary, and a dashboard must never see a night half loaded. Which item gives that guarantee?
hint: Three tables, one commit.

choices.text: A lakehouse, written by three Delta writes
choices.why: Each Delta write commits on its own, so a reader can land between two of them.

choices.text: A warehouse, loading all three in one transaction
choices.why: Right. A warehouse has multi-table transactions: a reader sees all of the night or none of it.

choices.text: A lakehouse's SQL analytics endpoint, with BEGIN and COMMIT
choices.why: The endpoint is read-only, so it cannot load anything.

choices.text: A shortcut to the database the shop writes to
choices.why: A shortcut points at files, and the guarantee is about how they are written.

prompt: Match each Fabric item to what it is.
hint: Two of them store the same format.

pairs.right: Delta tables written by Spark, beside a Files area
Delta tables owned by T-SQL, with multi-table transactions
Read-only T-SQL over a lakehouse's tables
A folder that points at data kept elsewhere

right_distractors: A pool of servers you size in DWUs and pause

prompt: How does a reader of the Delta table know which Parquet files are the table?
hint: It is not the folder listing.

choices.text: It lists the folder and reads every `.parquet` in it
choices.why: A file in the folder that no commit names is not in the table.

choices.text: From the footer of each Parquet file
choices.why: A footer describes its own file; it says nothing about the table.

choices.text: From the `add` actions in the commits of `_delta_log`
choices.why: Right. The log is the table: each `add` names a file, with its size and statistics.

choices.text: From the `protocol` action
choices.why: `protocol` says which features a reader must understand, not which files there are.

prompt: A colleague uploads a Parquet file of extra orders into `Tables/orders` by hand, with no commit. What does `ask.py` count afterwards?
hint: What reads the log, and what reads the folder?

choices.text: The same 98,727 orders
choices.why: Right. No `add` names the file, so for every Delta reader it is not there.

choices.text: 98,727 plus the extra orders, from the next read on
choices.why: That would be a reader listing the folder; `deltalake` reads the log.

choices.text: Nothing: the table refuses to open while a stray file is in its folder
choices.why: Readers ignore files the log does not name; they do not refuse the table.

choices.text: The extra orders only, since the newest file wins
choices.why: Delta has no rule about the newest file; only commits change the table.

prompt: DuckDB answered the question about payments without knowing the table was Delta. How?
hint: Two libraries split the work.

choices.text: DuckDB reads the JSON in `_delta_log` by itself
choices.why: In this program DuckDB never saw the log; it was given a dataset.

choices.text: `deltalake` read the log and handed it the files as one dataset
choices.why: Right. One library for the log, any engine for the files, which is why Fabric's engines share tables.

choices.text: Azurite turned the Delta table into plain Parquet on the way out
choices.why: Azurite stores blobs and knows nothing about Delta.

choices.text: The table has one file, so no log was needed
choices.why: The log was read whatever the number of files; that is how the file was found.

prompt: Each file in `_delta_log` is one commit, and each line of that file is one ___, such as `add` or `metaData`.
hint: The lesson lists four of them.

prompt: What does framing a Direct Lake semantic model do?
hint: It is fast because of what it does not move.

choices.text: Reads every row of the table into the model, as an import refresh does
choices.why: That is import mode; framing moves no data.

choices.text: Sends one SQL query per visual
choices.why: That is DirectQuery, which is where Direct Lake falls back to.

choices.text: Points the model at the table's latest version
choices.why: Right. It reads the newest commit of the log and copies no data, so it takes seconds.

choices.text: Rewrites the table's Parquet files with V-Order
choices.why: V-Order is applied when files are written, not by a report.

prompt: A Direct Lake report on Quitanda's orders grew slow over a month, with no error anywhere. The job writing the table appends a small file every five minutes. What is the likely cause?
hint: The guardrails count more than rows.

choices.text: The table passed a guardrail on files, and the model fell back to DirectQuery
choices.why: Right. Thousands of small files reach the guardrails long before the rows do, and fallback is quiet.

choices.text: Framing stopped, so the report is showing an old version
choices.why: An old version would be stale, not slow.

choices.text: The appended files carry V-Order, which slows reading
choices.why: V-Order exists to make reading faster.

choices.text: The capacity was paused overnight
choices.why: A paused capacity runs nothing at all; the report would fail, not slow.

prompt: Put Fabric's throttling stages in the order a capacity meets them as its carried-forward consumption grows.
hint: Ten minutes, an hour, a day.
items: Interactive delay: new interactive requests wait 20 seconds
Interactive rejection: new interactive requests are refused
Background rejection: every new request is refused

prompt: A background job uses 32 CUs for 45 minutes. Spread over 24 hours, how many CUs does it take on average?
hint: CU-seconds, divided by the 86,400 seconds of a day.
